fields.title: A release is a slice of a journey, not a set of features
fields.keyTakeaway: A good release allows the user to complete their task end-to-end, even if minimally. A release assembled from the "most ready" tasks often allows completing nothing.
fields.checkQuestion: The release includes: a new stock screen, scanner speedup, and export to 1C. What is wrong here?
fields.blocks/0/text: Key node question: **when to roll out changes to users?**
fields.blocks/1/text: **What happens if you don't answer the question.** The release is assembled from whatever got finished. The user gets half of a new process and half of an old one, while support gets tickets that didn't exist in either version.
fields.blocks/2/subtitle: Horizontal axis is the journey, vertical is depth
fields.blocks/2/items/0: **Top row** — task steps left to right: start inventory → scan → resolve divergence → close.
fields.blocks/2/items/1: **Under each step** — implementation options from simplest to rich.
fields.blocks/2/items/2: **A release is a horizontal slice** cutting across all steps. It is thin, but complete.
fields.blocks/2/items/3: **What this prevents:** the desire to perfect one step while leaving an adjacent step broken.
fields.blocks/3/text:
Bad: an excellent scanning screen with history, highlighting, and autocomplete. Meanwhile, there is nowhere to resolve divergence and no way to close the inventory. Unusable.

Good: scanning without history, divergence listed without filters, closing with file export. Modest at every step — yet the inventory is completed end-to-end, and two weeks later you can see exactly where people struggle.

In the second case, the next release is chosen based on observation, not personal taste.
fields.blocks/3/title: Polka, two ways to assemble the first release
fields.blocks/4/text: **It is useful to state release boundaries in words, not as a list of tasks.** "In this release, inventory can be completed end-to-end, but only for a single warehouse" — sales and support understand this formulation, and it naturally eliminates debatable tasks.
fields.blocks/5/text: The more changes go out at once, the harder it is to understand what broke and what worked. Frequent delivery is primarily a way to get feedback, not just speed.
fields.blocks/5/title: A large, infrequent release feels safer but is almost always more expensive
fields.blocks/6/text: A thin slice is no excuse for poor quality. Reduce scope and depth, not reliability: a broken half of a journey is worse than no journey at all.
